title: Removable Singularities Versus Vertical Asymptotes on Graphers
originalTopic: Graphing Technology: Hole Artifacts vs Asymptotes
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Contrast the graphical appearance on digital plotting software of f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) and g(x) = (x^2 + 1)/(x - 2) near x = 2.
finalAnswer: f(x) has a removable hole at (2, 4); g(x) has an infinite vertical asymptote at x = 2.

steps.title: Analyze the Factoring of f(x)
steps.explanation: Because the numerator and denominator share the common factor (x - 2), the singularity at x = 2 is removable. The graph is the line y = x + 2 with a single-point hole at (2, 4). On standard screen resolutions, this single missing pixel is often invisible.
steps.why: Cancellation of common factors converts rational fractions into polynomials with removable isolated point holes.

steps.title: Analyze the Behavior of g(x)
steps.explanation: At x = 2, the numerator of g(x) is 2^2 + 1 = 5 != 0, while the denominator approaches zero. The values grow without bound, creating an authentic vertical asymptote.
steps.why: A non-zero numerator divided by an infinitesimally small denominator produces infinite limits and true asymptotic behavior.

steps.title: Identify Grapher Screen Artifacts
steps.explanation: Simple graphers may deceptively display f(x) as an unbroken continuous line, while plotting a spurious vertical connecting segment across the asymptote of g(x).
steps.why: Screen pixel resolution and continuous line-drawing algorithms create visual misrepresentations of discontinuities.
